questions.prompt: Explain how the expense tracker keeps money values and record invariants valid, and why the rules live in the Expense constructor rather than only in the menu.

keyPoints.text: An invariant is a rule every accepted state must satisfy: positive id, nonblank title and category, valid date, positive two-place amount.
keyPoints.quote: An invariant is a rule that must hold for every accepted state.

keyPoints.text: The constructor enforces the rules because records arrive from both the menu and the saved file.
keyPoints.quote: The constructor enforces these rules because records can enter from either the menu or a file

keyPoints.text: Validating only menu input would leave the file-loading path unprotected.
keyPoints.quote: validating only menu input would leave the file-loading path unprotected.

keyPoints.text: Amounts use BigDecimal and setScale(2, UNNECESSARY), so a value that would need rounding is rejected instead of changed.
keyPoints.quote: silently rounding would change the accepted input

keyPoints.text: 12.300 is accepted because reducing its scale needs no rounding; 0.001, zero and negatives are rejected.
keyPoints.quote: `12.300` is accepted because reducing its scale to two requires no rounding.

keyPoints.text: Two decimal places is this teaching app's single-currency rule, not a universal truth; a real service should make currency explicit.
keyPoints.quote: This is a teaching application's single-currency rule, not a universal claim that every currency has two fractional digits.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an expense's identity and its contents, and how does updateExpense make a rejected edit leave everything unchanged?

keyPoints.text: Identity says which record this is; the editable fields say what it currently contains.
keyPoints.quote: Identity answers which record this is; editable fields answer what it currently contains.

keyPoints.text: Renaming Lunch to Bus keeps the same id so references stay meaningful.
keyPoints.quote: Changing Lunch to Bus must retain its ID so references remain meaningful.

keyPoints.text: updateExpense builds a complete candidate Expense before calling expenses.set.
If the date fails to parse, the old object stays and derived totals do not change.
keyPoints.quote: If parsing the date fails, the old object stays in the collection and all derived totals remain unchanged.

keyPoints.text: This is the small-scale version of validating a command before committing a database transaction.
keyPoints.quote: This pattern is the small-scale equivalent of validating a command before committing a database transaction.

questions.prompt: Where does an edit become durable in this app, what can still be lost or reused, how is a damaged file treated on load, and what does atomic file replacement not protect against? How should a change that needs two durable writes be fixed?

keyPoints.text: A copied list is only a collection snapshot, not a durable commit; edits stay in memory until the save.
keyPoints.quote: A copied list is a collection snapshot, not a durable commit.

keyPoints.text: A forced process termination can lose unsaved edits.
keyPoints.quote: A forced process termination can lose those unsaved edits.

keyPoints.text: No identity counter is persisted, so a deleted highest id can be reused after a restart.
keyPoints.quote: A deleted highest ID can therefore be reused across sessions

keyPoints.text: Whole-file validation: duplicate ids or one malformed line reject the entire load instead of a partial dataset.
keyPoints.quote: Duplicate IDs or a malformed line reject the entire load.

keyPoints.text: Atomic replacement stops readers seeing a half-written file, but gives no cross-process lock, no version check and no power-loss guarantee.
keyPoints.quote: It does not provide a cross-process lock, compare-and-swap version check, or guaranteed survival of power loss.

keyPoints.text: Two app instances can still overwrite each other's snapshots.
keyPoints.quote: Two app instances can still overwrite each other's snapshots.

keyPoints.text: A dual write (rows in one file, a counter in another) is fixed by making it one write, not by writing more carefully.
keyPoints.quote: The fix is never "write more carefully"; it is to make it one write
